s1.title: What is Parkinson's Disease?
s1.preview: A progressive neurological disorder that affects movement, mood, and sleep. Often years before tremors appear. Learn the early invisible symptoms most caregivers miss.
s1.p1: Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurological disorder that affects how the brain controls body movements. While most people immediately think of hand tremors or stiffness, Parkinson's is actually much more complex.
s1.p2: Research shows that Parkinson's affects more than just movement. In fact, many "invisible" symptoms can appear years before any walking difficulties begin. As a caregiver, you might notice your loved one experiencing:

items.title: Sleep Issues
items.desc: Acting out dreams, thrashing, or shouting during sleep

items.title: Mood Fluctuations
items.desc: Unexplained depression, anxiety, or lack of motivation

s1.outro: Knowing these issues are actual symptoms of Parkinson's and not just "normal aging" can help you provide more patient, empathetic care and communicate better with the neurologist.

s2.title: Recognizing Common Symptoms
s2.preview: Symptoms fall into motor and non-motor categories. Slowness of movement affects over 77% of patients. Non-motor symptoms often impact daily life even more than tremors.
s2.intro: Parkinson's symptoms vary from person to person, but they generally fall into two categories. Knowing what to look for helps you provide better care and keeps the doctor well-informed.

motorItems.title: Slowness of Movement
motorItems.desc: The most common symptom, affecting over 77% of patients. You might notice your parent taking longer to get dressed, walking with shorter steps, or struggling to stand up from a chair.

motorItems.title: Tremors
motorItems.desc: Shaking, usually starting in one hand while at rest.

motorItems.title: Stiffness
motorItems.desc: Muscles feel tight and inflexible, making it hard to swing their arms while walking.

motorItems.title: Balance & Gait Issues
motorItems.desc: Difficulty turning around, or feeling like their feet are "glued to the floor".

s2.nonMotorIntro: These symptoms are often overlooked but can affect daily life even more than motor symptoms.

nonMotorItems.title: Mood Changes
nonMotorItems.desc: Depression, apathy, and anxiety often appear together.

nonMotorItems.title: Sleep Problems
nonMotorItems.desc: Excessive daytime sleepiness, or acting out dreams at night.

nonMotorItems.title: Autonomic Issues
nonMotorItems.desc: Severe constipation, frequent/urgent urination, and feeling dizzy when standing up.

nonMotorItems.title: Pain & Fatigue
nonMotorItems.desc: Unexplained muscle aches and feeling constantly tired.

s2.tip: Log any of these symptoms in your ParkiCare Daily Record. It's crucial information for the neurologist!

s3.title: How Care Needs Change Over Time
s3.preview: Parkinson's progresses in stages. Your caregiver role shifts from encouraging independence in early stage to full-time physical assistance in late stage. Learn what to expect at each stage.
s3.intro: Parkinson's progresses differently for everyone. It is more helpful to understand how your loved one's needs and your role as a caregiver will change over time.
s3.earlyLook: Symptoms like tremors usually affect only one side of the body. You might notice they get tired more easily while walking.
s3.earlyRole: They can still live independently. Your main job is to help them establish a medication routine and encourage daily exercise.
s3.midLook: Symptoms affect both sides. They may experience "Freezing of Gait" and have trouble standing up from a chair or turning over in bed.
s3.midRole: Fall prevention is your top priority. They will need your physical assistance with daily tasks like dressing, bathing, and moving around the house safely.
s3.lateLook: Severe stiffness and mobility loss. They may require a wheelchair or become bedbound.
s3.lateRole: They need full-time assistance for all daily activities. Providing emotional, family, and spiritual comfort becomes just as important as physical care.

s4.title: Your Daily Observation Checklist
s4.preview: A practical guide to what to watch for every day, from medication "On/Off" timing and fall risks to invisible emotional fluctuations and mealtime safety.

groups.heading: 1. Medication Timing & "On/Off" Periods
items: Notice when the medication wears off before the next dose is due.

groups.heading: 2. Mobility & Fall Risks
items: Do their feet suddenly feel glued to the floor while walking?
Are they struggling to stand up from a chair, or having difficulty turning over in bed?
These are major fall risk warnings.

groups.heading: 3. The "Invisible" Fluctuations
items: Do they experience intense anxiety, sadness, or panic right before their next pill is due?
Note any sudden dizziness upon standing, severe pain, or excessive sleepiness during the day.

groups.heading: 4. Daily Care & Comfort
items: Do they have any choking, coughing, or swallowing difficulties during meals?
How many times do they wake up at night, and are they acting out their dreams?

s4.tip: Don't try to remember all of this! Use the ParkiCare Daily Record to quickly tap and save these observations as they happen.
sources: Source: Degenerative Neurological and Neuromuscular Disease, Volume 15, 101–116

s5.title: Why Your Tracking is the Doctor's Best Tool
s5.preview: Your neurologist sees your parent for only 15 minutes every few months. Your daily logs of symptoms, timing, and "Off" periods are what actually drive medication adjustments.
s5.p1: It's easy to feel like tracking daily symptoms is just "extra paperwork," but in Parkinson's care, your records are the actual medicine prescription.
s5.p2: Your neurologist only sees your parent for about 15 minutes every few months. They cannot see the sudden "Off" periods, the midnight hallucinations, or the non-motor anxiety crashes that happen at home.
s5.p3: Parkinson's treatment is highly individualized. Doctors rely entirely on your logs of "when symptoms worsen" to adjust the exact timing and dosage of Levodopa.
s5.highlight: By using the ParkiCare Daily Record, you are not just a caregiver; you are the doctor's most vital clinical partner.
sources: Source: Degenerative Neurological and Neuromuscular Disease, Volume 15, 101–116

s6.title: The Golden Rules of Medication
s6.preview: Parkinson's medications are time-critical, a 30-minute delay can cause severe "Off" periods or freezing. Learn the rules every caregiver must follow and never break.
s6.intro: Parkinson's medications are unlike typical blood pressure or vitamin pills. They are Time-Critical.

rules.title: Timing is Everything
rules.desc: Taking medication even 30 minutes late can cause a severe "Off" period, freezing of gait, or a sudden crash in mood/energy.

rules.title: Never Adjust Independently
rules.desc: Even if your parent is having a "bad day," never increase the dose or change the schedule without consulting the doctor.

rules.title: Set Persistent Reminders
rules.desc: Because household chores can be distracting, always rely on alarms.

s6.ctaButton: Tap here to set up your ParkiCare Persistent Medication Reminders now.

s7.title: Daily Care & Home Guidelines
s7.preview: Practical guidance on nutrition, constipation, swallowing, fall prevention, and exercise, the day-to-day practices that protect your loved one's health and safety at home.
s7.constipation: Ensure they drink 1.5 to 2 liters of water daily, and include plenty of fruits, vegetables, and olive oil in their diet.
s7.drooling: Drooling happens because of infrequent swallowing, not extra saliva. Encourage them to chew gum or use a "swallow timer" to practice swallowing more often.
s7.dizzy: Blood pressure drops are common when standing up. Teach them to rise very slowly from a bed or chair. Elevating the head of the bed by 30–45 degrees during sleep can also help.
s7.exercise: Regular physical activity, such as low-intensity walking or yoga, not only maintains mobility but also actively reduces Parkinson's-related pain.

s8.title: Red Flags - When to Call the Doctor
s8.preview: You are not expected to handle everything alone. Know the physical emergencies and mental health crises that require immediate professional intervention.
s8.intro: You are doing a great job, but you are not expected to handle everything alone. Contact your neurologist or seek immediate professional help if you observe any of the following:
s8.falls: If they feel light-headed or actually faint when standing up, their blood pressure medication may need urgent adjustment.
s8.choking: Any signs of silent aspiration (choking on saliva or food) require a speech-language therapist's intervention.
s8.hallucinations: Seeing things that aren't there (psychosis) is a severe complication that requires medication adjustments.
s8.burnoutLabel: Severe Caregiver Burnout or Patient Depression:
s8.burnout: If your loved one expresses a loss of "meaning in life" or you feel completely exhausted, please reach out to Parkinson's support groups, psychological counselors, or palliative care teams.

s9.title: BPT Caregiver Allowance (RM500/month)
s9.preview: Malaysian caregivers looking after bedridden or chronically ill patients may qualify for the BPT monthly financial allowance of RM500 from the Department of Social Welfare (JKM).
s9.imageAlt: Malaysian government financial assistance for caregivers
s9.intro: The Bantuan Pesakit Terlantar (BPT) programme provides RM500 per month to eligible caregivers who look after bedridden persons with disabilities or chronically ill patients in Malaysia.
s9.amountDesc: per month, distributed directly to the verified caregiver
eligItems: Caregiver for a bedridden person with disabilities (OKU)
Patient has a chronic illness requiring 3 or more months of continuous treatment
Bedridden patient with no other available Malaysian caregiver
Household monthly income does not exceed RM5,000
s9.howText: Applications are submitted online through the JKM e-Bantuan portal. JKM will verify your eligibility and confirm caregiver status before disbursement.
s9.contactAddr: Bangunan MKN Embassy Techzone, No. 3200 Jalan Teknokrat 2, 63000 Cyberjaya
s9.tip: Prepare medical documentation for the patient's condition and proof of household income before starting the online application.
s9.source: Source: Malaysia Government Portal — Assistance for Bedridden OKU / Chronically Ill Patients (BPT)

guide.title: How to Use ParkiCare
guide.subtitle: Step-by-step guide for caregivers
guide.notificationAlertPrefix: To receive medication alerts on iPhone, iPad, or Android:
guide.notificationAlertBody: add ParkiCare to your Home Screen. Tap Share → Add to Home Screen, then open the app from there and allow notifications when prompted.
guide.allSetDesc: Use the navigation links at the top to open Home, Care Events, or the Knowledge Hub anytime.
guide.feat1Subtitle: Add items and see today's priorities
guide.feat1Step1: Go to the Home page. Use the dashboard sections to add more medications, daily care tasks, or upcoming plans when needed.
guide.feat1Step2: Use this page to quickly see important medication times, care tasks, and scheduled events for today.
guide.feat1Step3Note: Use this page to quickly identify important medication times, care tasks, and scheduled events
guide.feat1Img1Alt: Home dashboard - add medications, care tasks, and plans
guide.feat1Img2Alt: Calendar view - use Week or Month and the Today control to see medications, care tasks, and scheduled events
guide.feat2Subtitle: Scan, review, save, and respond to reminders
guide.feat2Step1: Open Care Events and use Add Medication on the left. The form is a short wizard (photo → name → dosage → dates & repeat → how often & meal timing → dose times → review).
guide.feat2Step2: Optional photo of the label - ParkiCare shows a short OCR-style processing screen, then displays a suggestion panel only; it does not auto-fill the form fields.
guide.feat2Step3: Enter the drug (search the list or type the name), then dosage (oral strength/quantity or another route), start/end dates, repeat, frequency, when to take (with meals), and administration times.
guide.feat2Step4: On the Review step, check everything and tap Confirm & Save to add it to your Medication List and schedule.
guide.feat2Step5: When a reminder appears, use Confirm Administration or Snooze 5 min as needed.
guide.feat2Img1Alt: Care Events - add home care tasks and review activities
guide.feat3Subtitle: Daily care tasks and upcoming activities
guide.feat3Step1: Go to Care Events and open the Add Care Event section to manage daily caregiving activities.
guide.feat3Step2: Add tasks or events such as bathing, nursing care, appointments, or household-related responsibilities.
guide.feat3Step3: Use this area to keep track of important plans and daily care responsibilities.
guide.feat4Subtitle: Plan outings and see them on your schedule
guide.feat4Step1: From the navigation menu, open the Care Events page.
guide.feat4Step2: Select Add Outdoor Event to create a new outdoor event.
guide.feat4Step3: Enter the event title, category or type, and event time.
guide.feat4Step4: Tap Save Outdoor Event to add it to your care schedule.
guide.feat4Step5: The event appears in your care planning section for easier daily management.
guide.feat4Img1Alt: Outdoor event saved on the care schedule
guide.feat5Step1: After you log in, your browser may ask to allow notifications for ParkiCare. Choose Allow so medication reminders can reach you on time.
guide.feat5Step2: If you dismissed the prompt or chose Block, open the site settings for ParkiCare in your browser and set Notifications to Allow.
guide.feat5Step3: When a medication reminder fires, you may get a system notification and an in-app prompt to Confirm Administration or Snooze.
guide.feat5Step4: Push works well on Android and on desktop browsers such as Chrome, Edge, and Firefox.
guide.feat5Step4Note: On iPhone or iPad, add ParkiCare to the Home Screen and use a recent iOS version; enable notifications in system settings if prompted.
guide.feat6Step1: Open Knowledge Hub from the top navigation.
guide.feat6Step2: Watch the introductory video and read the topic cards for fundamentals of Parkinson's care.
guide.feat6Step3: Use the references section for links to deeper reading.
